transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Janine Herbst.
Ukrainian President Zelensky has branded Vladimir Putin a "killer"
after President Trump referred to the Russian leader as his "friend" this week.
And here's Eleanor Beardsley, Hasmore.
In response to a question about Trump referring to Putin as his friend, Zelensky told CNN...
For us, he's an enemy. And of course, for us, he's a killer.
...Trump made the comment as he and Putin met alongside China's Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.
Trump continued to talk up his relationship with the Russian dictator during a press conference at the White House on Friday.
On Thursday night, Russian forces launched a major wave of strikes against Ukraine,
killing at least seven people in Kiev and damaging key bridges across the Nipro River.
Zelensky said Russia had fired more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles during the assault,
which he called one of the largest attacks of the war so far.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Lviv, Ukraine.
The big slide in AI shares and the broader stock market is raising concerns about
whether we're in the midst of a financial bubble that might end badly.
NPR's Rafael Naum has more.
AI companies such as Nvidia have powered the stock market for years.
But a string of recent problems in the AI sector are raising concerns about whether investors will see the returns they were expecting.
The fear is that we could be in the midst of a financial bubble, similar to the dot-com era of the 1990s,
since AI companies have become such an essential part of financial markets and the wider economy.
Some analysts fear it could be even worse. AI companies have borrowed massive amounts of money.
And travel in one or two companies could spark a chain reaction that could even lead to a financial crisis.
Rafael Naum, NPR News.
The agrochemical company Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued the company,
alleging the weed killer Roundup caused their cancer. And Piers Willstone reports,
a judge in Missouri approved the settlement yesterday.
Bayer could pay as much as seven and a quarter billion dollars in the coming years.
That money will go to people who already have non-Hodgkin lymphoma or get diagnosed in the future.
In his statement, the CEO of Bayer called the settlement a decisive milestone that will mitigate pending and future litigation.
The World Health Organization's cancer agency has found that glyphosate, the main ingredient in the company's weed killer Roundup,
is probably carcinogenic to humans. Prominent scientists in the field of environmental health have echoed those concerns.
But the company denies this is the case, and the Environmental Protection Agency has also said it does not pose a risk to human health,
though the agency is currently reevaluating that finding. Willstone, NPR News.
And you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
In Mexico, at least 11 people were killed in Sinaloa State after authorities captured the cartel boss known as El Chapo Isidro.
Mexico's defense cabinet says seven alleged cartel gunmen and four soldiers were killed in the firefight that erupted last night.
El Chapo Isidro is one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, and he was among eight people arrested in the operation,
which was carried out using intelligence from the United States.
In a world-first, researchers say they've been able to sequence the entire genome of a humpback whale using its nasal mucus.
And Pierre's Nate Rott has more.
So how does one collect whale snot, you ask?
Careful timing.
And drones.
The drones have got sterile petri dishes attached to them, literally velcroed on.
And then as that whale comes up and breathes out...
Splatter.
Ecologist Aideen Omani and fellow scientists collected dozens of samples from humpback whales in northern British Columbia.
And a new study shows they were able to use those snot samples to sequence a whole whale genome,
which can tell scientists a lot about the health of the entire species.
All in a non-invasive, albeit stickier way.
Nate Rott, NPR News.
Both Honda and Toyota are recalling around 1.6 million vehicles because the Takata airbag inflators could rupture.
Both of the automakers say no injuries or crashes and nor airbag inflator ruptures have been reported.
I'm Janine Herbst, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Zelensky calls Putin a killer after Trump calls him his friend
Russia launches major overnight strike on Ukraine, killing at least seven in Kyiv
AI stock slide raises fears of a financial bubble and possible crisis
Bayer agrees to pay up to $7.25 billion to settle Roundup cancer lawsuits
Mexican forces capture cartel boss El Chapo Isidro in Sinaloa; at least 11 killed
Scientists sequence full humpback whale genome using nasal mucus collected by drones
Honda and Toyota recall 1.6 million vehicles over Takata airbag inflator rupture risk
